senses: A racehorse that performs well on muddy or wet tracks.
A person who handles, works with, digs or is otherwise involved in mud.
A yokai with the head of a human and the body of a bovine.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 件 (kudan), which consists of the two radicals 亻 (“person”) + 牛 (“cow”).

senses: The state of being incongruous or surreal.
That which is surreal; a surreal entity, event or other fact.
examples: The surreality of the crash scene dawned upon him only when he saw a holy figure in the smoke.
And when he goes to greet his mother the surreality of it all stares him in the face: in two years she's turned into a little old lady.
The surrealities of life are the paradoxes thereof.

senses: To flop down wearily.
To fall down dead.
ety: From Yiddish פּלאַצן (platsn, “to split, crack, burst, explode”).

senses: A tumour, often accompanied by inflammation; pustule; varicose vein; pus; atter.
A defect or flaw, especially in cloth.
ety: From Middle English ampre, from Old English ampre (“a dilated vein, varix, tumour, swelling; dock, sorrel”), from Proto-West Germanic *amprō, *amprā (“dock, sorrel”), which is related to Proto-Germanic *ampraz (“sharp”). Related to aber.

senses: An indentation; a recess.
ety: From Anglo-Norman endenture, from Old French endenteure, from endenter (“to dent”). The name of the contract derives from the irregular dent-shaped cut (indentation) used to prove the authenticity of the two parts, similar to a chirograph.

senses: Fabric woven on a Jacquard loom.
Fabric resembling a jacquard, but woven by a different process.
A Jacquard loom.
ety: Eponym, from Joseph Marie Jacquard, inventor of the Jacquard loom.
examples: The White House has jacquard drapes in the East Room.

senses: the state of being erotic, or of being sexually aroused
sexual excitement, especially if abnormally persistent
a sexual interest in something; an attraction, fetish, etc.
The polymerization of multiple monomers to form a copolymer
Densely packed crushed rock covering the ground where a bullfight will take place.
The act of uniting by glue or other tenacious substance; the state of being thus united; adhesion of parts.
The clumping together of red blood cells or bacteria, usually in response to a particular antibody.
To make concrete, substantial, real, or tangible; to represent or embody a concept through a particular instance or example.
To be embodied, to have physical representation.
examples: An essence exists if and only if it is actualized or concretized somehow, in some concrete form.
But Ms. Yauger's death concretized these abstract discussions and theories.
Rights in this way stem from social conventions that concretize and shape the values that underlie them.

senses: vigorously active
Having many centres, especially centres of authority or control
examples: When applied to other persons, the idea of comfort is an intuitive measure of trustworthiness, reliability, and predictability in a polycentric world that managers often find troubling, ambiguous, and anxiety-laden.

senses: Having twelve plane surfaces.
The tendency to represent eastern subjects, to assume stylistical characteristics original of the East, especially in 19th century Europe.
An Eastern word, expression, or custom.
A patronizing Western attitude towards Middle Eastern, Asian, and North African societies.
ety: From French orientalisme, from oriental (“eastern, Oriental”). In the sense “patronizing Western attitude” popularized by Edward Said's 1978 book Orientalism. Equivalent to Oriental + -ism.
examples: The Scriptural style and the Scriptural language are not meant for one age, but for all ages. Its orientalisms will grow in the west; its archaisms will be found still young in the nineteenth century.

senses: The act of making or becoming gelatinous.
unlawful; illegal.
examples: We have a place for lawbreaking citizens like you.
To make this penalty hang like a Sword of Damocles over every lawbreaking alien apprehended in this country
Although church leaders argue they're trying to help the most vulnerable in society, some, including parishioners, argue they're helping the most lawbreaking.

senses: The view that a text should be interpreted according to the intent of its original authors.
examples: One of the points that you’ve made in the past is that when originalism was first taking hold as a popular theory, one of the reasons for its popularity was that it was seen as offering a kind of restraint on justices.

senses: A belief, expressed by survivalists, in being prepared to survive disasters and cataclysms including the collapse of civilization; the practice of preparing for such events.
Pronounced with every syllable distinct.
Of, or being a form of verse, based on the number of syllables in a line rather than on the arrangement of accents or quantities.
ety: From Medieval Latin syllabicus, from Ancient Greek συλλαβικός (sullabikós), from συλλαβή (sullabḗ, “syllable”).

senses: To represent (someone or something) in a particular style.

To represent (someone or something) abstractly in a conventional manner, commonly fancifully symbolic, to identify a particular item, by omitting most of the detail that is not unique to the item in question.
ety: From style + -ize. Probably from German stilisieren.

senses: The plant muskroot.
Capable of being rebutted.
A person who carries a cross in a religious procession, a cross bearer.
ety: From Latin crucifer (“cross-bearer”), from crux (“cross”) + ferō (“to carry, bear”).

senses: That can be inhaled.
One who studies musicology.
A measurable quantity capable of taking on a number of values.
A variable, often the set of x values plotted on a graph.
The measured magnitude of a variable.
ety: From Latin variatus, past participle of variare. See vary.

senses: mantis (insect)
A mantis in the family Mantidae.
Someone who plays the cornet.
examples: The cornetist’s sombre repertoire had made her spirits drop.

senses: A group of illustrious or talented people, especially one with seven members.
ety: Probably from the English Pleiades, divine sisters in Greek mythology who were believed to have been placed in the heavens as a well known group of seven stars.

senses: Synonym of Eskimo kiss.
Blazing; resembling or characteristic of a blaze.
A powdered form of impure zinc oxide used for polishing.
ety: From French tutie; compare Spanish tutía, atutía, from Latin tutia, from Arabic تُوتِيَاء (tūtiyāʔ), from Classical Persian توتیا (tūtyā), from Sanskrit तुत्था (tutthā).

senses: A facility that carries out coproduction of a range of biologically-based products (food, feed, materials, chemicals) and energy (fuels, power, heat) from biomass.
The coproduction process itself.
Characteristic of a painter or paintings.
Having clear brush-strokes.
Forming a pair.
ety: First attested in 1589; borrowed from Latin geminātus, perfect passive participle of geminō (“to double”), see -ate (etymology 1,2 and 3).

senses: a motorized cultivator having rotating blades
ety: From a trade name, from rotary tiller.

senses: A drink made of espresso coffee diluted with hot water.
A cocktail made with Campari, sweet vermouth, and club soda.
ety: 1970s, from Italian (caffè) americano or American Spanish americano (“American (coffee)”). Cocktail sense from Italian americano.
examples: And he drank americano. That was interesting. Was he lactose intolerant or did he simply prefer his coffee black?

senses: compensation paid for such detention
a charge made for exchanging currency for bullion
the cost associated with owning or holding currency over a given period
a type of currency which requires paying a fee to store money; a type of currency that discourages using money as a store of value
ety: 1640s, from Old French demorage, from demorer (English demur), from Latin dēmorārī (“to tarry”). By surface analysis, demur (“delay”) + -age, with doubled ‘r’ to clarify pronunciation and avoid ambiguity with demure.
